thread.title: Amazon Vs. Facebook: This Is No Contest - Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN)

author: Robert Riesen
title: Amazon Vs. Facebook: This Is No Contest - Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN)
text:
With each stock trading near all-time highs, both Facebook ( FB ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) have performed well so far this year. Both continue to be on a torrid growth path, but that's where I see the similarities stop. I consider Facebook the perfect stock. Sure, the Cambridge data debacle has been a public relations nightmare, but if you look at only performance, it would be hard to find a better company. Facebook's combination of operating performance, growth rate, balance sheet, and valuation are pretty much second to none. Where Amazon excels is its potential, but this is speculative and greatly increases the stock's risk. For Amazon's stock price to make sense, some pretty outrageous assumptions need to be made and it's still unclear if or when the company can make those achievements.
Operating Performance - Winner: Facebook Facebook has significantly less revenue, but higher operating margins allow them to produce larger profits. In 2017, Facebook produced $20.2 billion in operating profit versus only $4.1 billion in operating profit for Amazon. Keep in mind that Amazon is valued at a higher level (Enterprise Value of $852 billion versus $523 billion for Facebook), so Facebook's lead on operating profit is more significant than just looking at the numbers. Facebook also grew sales by 47% during 2017, which is also favorable to Amazon at 31%.
Data Source: Amazon's SEC Filings
Data Source: Facebook's SEC Filings Free Cash Flow - Winner: Facebook Free cash flow is the most important operating metric and is at the core of how I analyze stocks since it drives investments, acquisitions, dividends, stock repurchases, and debt levels. Facebook produced twice the amount of free cash flow than Amazon did during 2017 and is off to a much faster start in 2018.
Balance Sheet - Winner: Facebook Both companies have good balance sheets, but Facebook's is much better. Facebook has already built a cash war chest and has no debt. I see Facebook as one of the few companies that has a chance of taking over Apple ( AAPL ) as the cash king over the next decade. Amazon has taken on debt, which increased considerably during 2017 given the Whole Foods acquisition and other investments. While $44 billion in debt is minuscule relative to its enterprise value, the rate at which debt is increasing could pose some concern in the future.
Valuation - Winner: Facebook If Facebook hasn't separated itself from Amazon enough already, things really become clear when comparing valuations. With Facebook, you get a similar growth rate, but valuations that are significantly cheaper across the board. Facebook also looks cheap relative to other high-growth technology companies given a PEG Ratio of only 1x. I've often contested that Amazon's valuations are highly speculative and based on performance that the company might not achieve for another 5 to 10 years. As an example, for Amazon to have an EV/FCF of 25x, it needs to produce free cash flow of $34 billion, which isn't going to occur for a long time.
Enterprise Value, Forward P/E, and PEG Ratio provided by Yahoo Finance . EV/FCF provided by Ycharts LT Growth Rate derived from Forward P/E and PEG Ratio Averages for Forward P/E, EV/FCF, and PEG Ratio do not include Amazon Wall Street's Opinion - Winner: Draw Wall Street has very similar ratings on both Facebook and Amazon. Target prices represent the same amount of upside potential and an identical amount of analysts rate each stock as a 'Buy'. According to MarketWatch , the average target price for Facebook is $221.32, which represents 10% upside based on the current share price of $201.59. The average target price for Amazon is $1,885, which represents 10% upside based on the current share price of $1,717.
Risk Profile - Winner: Facebook I believe there is now tremendous risk in Amazon's valuation returning back to historical averages. A large percentage of the stock price increase has been a result of increasing Price/Sales multiples, which is now at 4.4x (a crazy number for an e-commerce company). Amazon's EV/FCF has also trended in the same direction. Facebook's stock does not have this risk. Not only are its current Price/Sales, Forward Earnings, and EV/FCF very reasonable, they are all below 3-year averages. Facebook trades near an all-time high, yet valuation multiples have gone down. This is an important distinction between the two stocks since each has reached all-time highs, but Facebook's has been more performance based.
AMZN PS Ratio (TTM) data by YCharts AMZN EV to Free Cash Flow (TTM) data by YCharts FB PS Ratio (TTM) data by YCharts FB PS Ratio (TTM) data by YCharts Conclusion In my opinion, there's a number of factors that make Facebook look much more attractive when compared to Amazon:
Facebook trades cheaper at every major valuation multiple. In particular, a significantly lower PEG ratio is compelling. Facebook's enterprise value is less than Amazon's, but produces better profits, better free cash flow, has a better balance sheet, and a similar level of long-term growth. Facebook produces double the amount of free cash flow, is quickly amassing a cash war chest, and has no debt. Facebook's stock has earned its stock price purely through strong performance, which is identifiable through its 3-year valuation multiple trends. Facebook has tremendous untapped potential, but the stock is valued on today's performance. Any untapped potential will likely yield additional upside in the stock. Disclosure: I am/we are long FB AAPL.
